name: Anti-wrinkle pillow
lead: Anti-wrinkle pillows are contoured, cut-out or cushioned pillows, and smooth pillowcases made of silk, satin or similar fabrics, sold to reduce pressure and creasing of the face against bedding during sleep. People use them to keep the forehead, cheeks and chest from picking up lines while they sleep, aiming for smoother-looking skin over the years.[3]

The premise is that sleep wrinkles form when the face is pressed, stretched and compressed against a pillow, particularly in side and stomach sleepers. Researchers at the University of Queensland writing in The Conversation describe sleep wrinkles as creases that usually fade soon after waking in younger skin but can become lasting lines as skin loses elasticity, and note that people who always sleep on one side often show more lines on that side.[3] Wikipedia lists habitual sleeping position among the factors that can contribute to skin wrinkling, alongside ageing, sun damage, smoking, weight loss and facial expressions.[1]

The same Conversation article says pillows designed to reduce mechanical stress on the face may help limit skin deformation in sleep, and that smooth fabrics such as silk may help if they let skin glide rather than drag.[3] No published clinical trial of anti-wrinkle pillow products was located, so product claims rest on this mechanical theory and manufacturer descriptions.

chain: Pillow shape or smooth cover reduces pressure and drag on the face
Less repeated creasing in the same facial areas
Fewer or fainter sleep lines over time
angle.text: Users buy these pillows to cut nightly compression of the face, expecting sleep lines on the cheeks, forehead and chest to be shallower. The routine works alongside other approaches commonly described for wrinkles, such as sunscreen and moisturizing.[3]

infobox: Contoured pillow or smooth pillowcase intended to reduce facial compression
Less facial pressure and shear; lower friction for silk-type covers[3]
Sleeping on the back or changing positions[3]

paras: Designs include pillows with cut-outs or channels that let the cheek or forehead rest without contact, cradle-shaped or wedge pillows that encourage back sleeping, and flat pillowcases of silk, satin or copper-infused fabric intended to let skin glide. Pillows in general are bedding items designed for head and neck support and comfort, in varied shapes, sizes and fillings.[2]

The Queensland authors say pressing the face into a pillow stretches, compresses and pulls the skin, especially for side and stomach sleepers, and that both sleeping position and how much the face moves against the pillow affect where and how quickly lines form.[3] Wikipedia describes the misrepair-accumulation theory of ageing, in which wrinkles develop from incorrect repair of elastic and collagen fibres injured by repeated extension and compression of the skin.[1] Proponents of anti-wrinkle pillows apply this idea to hours of nightly facial compression.[3]

The same article lists sleeping on the back or changing positions overnight, moisturizing before bed, ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, and general measures such as sun protection, not smoking and hydration.[3] Wikipedia lists sun exposure, smoking and ageing as promoters of wrinkling.[1]

No studies found of anti-wrinkle pillows or silk pillowcases for wrinkle outcomes. The Conversation article draws on research about skin ageing, sleep position and facial pressure, and pillow design in general rather than trials of these products.[3]
Risks are low. Reported downsides are discomfort or disturbed sleep from an unfamiliar shape, and cost.

Within skin-care and appearance communities, sleeping position is discussed as a cause of facial lines, with back sleeping suggested as a no-cost alternative to specialised pillows. The Conversation article was also posted to Hacker News in 2024 under the title 'Sleep Wrinkles Are Real'.[3][4] Specialised pillows and silk cases are commonly priced from roughly $40 to $100.
